title: Mass spectrometry of elements; Empirical and molecular formulae; States of matter and phase changes
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AS02#t2 term and clue written for the game; AS02#t1 term and clue written for the game; AS02#t3 term and clue written for the game; AM02#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM02#N.3, AS02#N.6b, BD08#N.2b, AM02#N.5, AS02#N.6c, BD08#N.5, AM02#N.7b, AS02#N.13, BD08#N.8b, AM02#N.11, BD08#N.11, BD08#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Mass-to-charge ratio
items.clue: The quantity written m/z, plotted on the x-axis of the spectrum.

items.label: Mass spectrometer
items.clue: Instrument that turns particles into positive ions and sorts them.

items.label: Relative abundance
items.clue: Shown by peak height: how much of each isotope an element contains.

items.label: Molecular formula
items.clue: Shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one unit, e.g. C₂H₄ or H₂O₂.

questions.stem: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its molar mass is 60.05 g/mol. What is the empirical formula of the compound?

options.text: CH₂O
C₆HO₈
CHO
C₂H₄O₂

questions.explanation: In 100 g: 3.33 mol C, about 6.6–6.7 mol H, 3.33 mol O. ÷ smallest: 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of a sample of a hypothetical element Z shows three peaks, with heights given relative to the tallest peak: 28 amu (100), 29 amu (8.0) and 30 amu (4.0). What is the average atomic mass of Z in the sample, in amu?
Which of the numbered diagrams represents a pure substance?

options.text: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4

questions.explanation: Every particle is the same CO₂ molecule, so the sample is a pure substance.

questions.stem: A compound of aluminium and sulfur contains 35.93% aluminium and 64.07% sulfur by mass. What is its empirical formula? Data: Al 26.98, S 32.06.

options.text: AlS
Al₃S₂
AlS₂
Al₂S₃

questions.explanation: Divide each mass by its atomic mass: Al 1.33, S 2.00. Ratio 1 : 1.50; × 2 = 2 : 3.

questions.stem: A laboratory prepares a sample of magnesium in which the proportions of the three isotopes of magnesium differ from those in natural magnesium. Which information is needed to calculate the average atomic mass of magnesium in this sample?

options.text: The masses of all three isotopes and the number of isotopes
The atomic mass given for magnesium on the periodic table
The mass of the isotope giving the tallest mass-spectrum peak
The mass and the relative abundance of each isotope in the sample

questions.explanation: Multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance in this sample, then add.

questions.stem: For a typical substance at 1 atm, how does the molar volume of the solid at its melting point compare with the molar volume of the liquid at the same temperature?

options.text: The two are similar, because the particles are in close contact in both phases.
The liquid's is much larger, because its particles are spread well apart.
The solid's is larger, because solids are typically less dense than their liquids.
The solid's is much smaller, because the particles in a solid are smaller.

questions.explanation: Particles touch their neighbors in both phases, so a mole occupies a similar volume; typically a few percent different.

questions.stem: A student has found the empirical formula of a molecular compound from its percent composition by mass. Which additional quantity does the student need in order to determine the compound's molecular formula?

options.text: None; the empirical formula is also the molecular formula
The total mass of the sample of the compound analyzed
The molar mass of the compound, found by another method
The atomic numbers of the elements in the compound

questions.explanation: Molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass gives the whole-number multiple.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of gallium shows two peaks from 1+ ions: m/z 69 (height 100) and m/z 71 (height 66.4). What is the average atomic mass of gallium given by these data, in amu?

A pot of water is boiling steadily over a burner, and a thermometer in the water reads 100 °C throughout. A student claims that the boiling water is not absorbing energy from the burner. Which statement best evaluates the claim?

options.text: The claim is correct; absorbing energy would make the water hotter, but this water stays at 100 °C
The claim is incorrect; the energy absorbed breaks the O–H bonds in the water molecules as they boil
The claim is incorrect; the water absorbs energy as it changes from liquid to gas, so its energy increases
The claim is correct; the burner's energy is carried away by bubbles of air rising out of the water

questions.stem: Ethyne, a welding gas, and benzene, a liquid, both contain 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen by mass. What is the molecular formula of benzene? Data: H 1.008, C 12.01. Molar mass of benzene = 78.11 g/mol.

options.text: CH
C₁₂H
C₆H₆
C₂H

questions.explanation: C: 92.3 ÷ 12 ≈ 7.7; H: 7.7 ÷ 1 ≈ 7.7. Ratio 1 : 1, empirical formula CH (about 13). x = 78 ÷ 13 = 6: C₆H₆.

questions.stem: The molar enthalpy of vaporization of water at 100 °C is 40.7 kJ/mol. How much energy is released when 1.60 g of steam at 100 °C condenses to liquid water at 100 °C?
questions.explanation: n = 1.60 ÷ 18.02 = 0.0888 mol. Condensing releases what vaporizing absorbs: 0.0888 × 40.7 = 3.61 kJ.

questions.stem: A drop of steam at 100 °C on the skin causes a far worse burn than a drop of the same mass of water at 100 °C. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Steam molecules at 100 °C have a higher average kinetic energy than water molecules at 100 °C.
Steam releases its enthalpy of vaporisation as it condenses on the skin, then cools like the water.
Steam contains hydrogen and oxygen, which react on the skin and release energy.
Steam is a gas, so each gram of it stores more energy per degree than liquid water does.

questions.explanation: 18 g of steam releases about 41 kJ just by condensing. Cooling 18 g of water from 100 °C to 37 °C releases only about 5 kJ more.
